Contempt

kun-TEMPT — rhymes with 'attempt'; contempt attempts no respect at all. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Contempt is a feeling that someone or something deserves scorn or is beneath respect.

The senator's contempt for the reporters' questions was obvious from his dismissive tone.

Worked Example

A judge listens to a witness lie under oath, repeatedly and shamelessly, even after being caught. The judge's expression hardens, and she refuses to look at the witness for the rest of the hearing.

The judge's total lack of respect for someone she considers dishonest and worthless is contempt. Unlike 'anger,' which is a hot, active emotion, contempt is a cold, dismissive sense that someone doesn't even deserve a reaction.

How Contempt Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

scorn

scorn: open contempt or disdain

disdain

disdain: a feeling that someone is unworthy of respect

derision

derision: contemptuous ridicule or mockery

Antonyms

admiration

admiration: respect and warm approval

reverence

reverence: deep, awed respect

How Strong Is It? — dislike → contempt → loathing

dislike vs. contempt

dislike vs. contempt: Dislike is weaker than contempt — you can dislike something without judging it as worthless, while contempt adds that cold sense that it doesn't even deserve respect.

loathing vs. contempt

loathing vs. contempt: Loathing is stronger than contempt: contempt is a cold, dismissive judgment, but loathing is a hot, intense revulsion.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — con- (com-)

prefix — con- (com-): intensive (Latin)

root — -tempt- (-temn-)

root — -tempt- (-temn-): to scorn, to despise (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin contemnere meant 'to scorn utterly.' Contempt is that same feeling — treating someone or something as beneath notice or worthless.

Use the root in a new word: contemptible

Use the root in a new word: contemptible: Cheating on the exam was a contemptible act that cost him his classmates' trust.
